title: Naam: the Name
hook: Naam is more than a word; it is the presence of the One, remembered until it fills you

segments.voice: Yesterday, haumai, the I-me. Your line was the cure is inside. Did you catch a me-first moment and turn it around? Today, the medicine the Granth names most often. Day two hundred thirty-seven.

Think of how many ways your name gets said. Read off a list at the dentist's office: flat, just a label. Shouted across a parking lot: a signal. And then the way someone who loves you says it, maybe a parent when you were small, or a grandparent who's gone now. That voice didn't just identify you. It held you. If you heard it again right now, something in your chest would open. Same name, completely different thing. A name, said a certain way, carries a whole presence with it. Sikhs have a word for the Name of the One. And they mean it that second way.
screen: `A NAME READ OFF A LIST.` → `A NAME SAID WITH LOVE.` → `A NAME THAT CARRIES A PRESENCE.`

segments.voice: Today's word is naam. Literally, name. But in the Granth, naam is far more than a word for God. It's the presence of the One, running through everything, which a person can remember until it fills them. You've heard it from the very beginning. The Mool Mantar calls the One Satnam: truth is the Name. Pauri 4 of the Japji says in the ambrosial early hours, reflect on the true Name. And Pauri 19 has one of the boldest lines in the whole bani: jetaa keetaa tetaa naaou. As much as has been made, that much is the Name. Vin naavai naahee ko thaaou: without the Name, there's no place at all. So naam isn't a label stuck onto creation. Creation is where the Name shows up. That's why the Granth keeps coming back to it. Naam japo, remember the Name, is one of three simple pillars many Sikhs are taught from childhood, alongside honest work and sharing with others. Naam simran, remembering the Name, can mean repeating Waheguru, or singing hymns, or simply holding the One in mind while you chop onions or drive to work. And yesterday's riddle, the disease with its own cure? Many Sikh teachers say naam is the medicine. When the Name fills you, there's less room for the I-me. It isn't pushed out by force. It's more like a room filling with light: the shadows don't lose a fight; they just aren't there anymore.
screen: `NAAM — MORE THAN A LABEL.` · `SATNAM — TRUTH IS THE NAME.` · `JETAA KEETAA TETAA NAAOU.` · `THE NAME AS THE MEDICINE.` · then, large: `THE NAME FILLS YOU.`

segments.voice: Rest for this whole sit in one quiet stretch. No task, no counting. If you'd like, on a slow breath in, let the word Waheguru rise silently, and on the breath out, let it settle. If that word isn't yours, simply rest in the quiet, the way you'd sit in a room with someone you love without needing to talk. Let whatever presence you feel fill the space, slowly, like light. The bell holds the time.
Naam. The Name: not a label but the presence of the One, in everything that's made, remembered until it fills you.
Your line: the name fills you. Today, during one ordinary task, washing up or walking, hold the One quietly in mind, and see what fills the room. Day two hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs practice naam simran by repeating Waheguru, singing kirtan, or holding the One in mind through the day; naam japo, remembering the Name, is taught alongside kirat karo, honest work, and vand chhako, sharing.

trapdoor: what you thought: naam means God's name, like a label.
what it means: the presence of the One in everything, remembered until it fills you.
what a scholar hears: Japji 19 equates the Name with all creation, jetaa keetaa tetaa naaou; naam simran is taught as the medicine for haumai.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (Mool Mantar); Ang 2 (Japji, Pauri 4)

notes: Gurmukhi quoted in transliteration as the original; English is paraphrase.
Ang 4 for Japji Pauri 19 and Ang 2 for Pauri 4; confirm.
The three pillars (naam japo, kirat karo, vand chhako) are a traditional summary of Guru Nanak's teaching rather than a single Granth line; described as what many Sikhs are taught.
'Many Sikh teachers say naam is the medicine' for haumai is common teaching; confirm.
